methodology.title: Curated source-first AI intelligence brief
methodology.summary: This dataset is generated from public source feeds. Items are linked back to their original URLs, timestamped, and auto-categorized for triage rather than treated as infallible truth.
caveats: Feed freshness depends on source publication latency and RSS availability.
Threads coverage uses RSSHub adapters and may fail or lag if the upstream route changes.
Automatic categorization is heuristic and should be reviewed for decision-critical workflows.

research.title: When Do Rankings Beat Signs? Gradient Direction Recovery under Even Nuisance
research.summary: Can ranking a batch of antipodal query pairs recover a gradient direction with fewer evaluations than using within-pair signs alone? We study fixed-center recovery in $d$ dimensions for a linear signal plus an unknown differentiable even nuisance, counting function evaluations and feedback rounds separately. Shared pair offsets create an information hierarchy: Mirror retains within-pair signs, Reverse couples reversed cross-pair orders to cancel offsets, and Full enforces all ranking inequalities. Relative shell variation is the nuisance range over the query sphere normalized by the linear-signal scale. When it is at most $c\varepsilon/\sqrt{d}$, Reverse localizes every consistent direction to angular accuracy $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde{O}(d+\sqrt{d/\varepsilon})$ evaluations in one round at fixed confidence, without a variation bound supplied to the decoder. This matches a lower bound up to logarithmic factors, versus the $Θ(d/\varepsilon)$ one-round sign-only minimax cost on the same class. Over well-conditioned positive-definite quadratics with no common relative-curvature bound, the $R$-round minimax cost is instead $Θ(dR(\varepsilon^{-1/R}-1))$, even with cumulative rankings. We extend validity beyond exact evenness under supplied error bounds. Matched-endpoint experiments certify information beyond signs and short cycles. On two ridge tasks under joint evaluation and round caps, short-cycle recovery attains lower terminal mean gaps than the tested batch-capable controls. An additional optimization benefit from fitting the complete ranking remains unestablished.

research.title: Reference-Free Humanoid Skateboarding via Termination-Shaped Reinforcement Learning
research.summary: Humanoid locomotion research has advanced rapidly on walking and running, but \emph {object-mediated} locomotion, in which a robot must coordinate its body with a passive external object, remains difficult. One challenging task is skateboarding, which requires simultaneous interaction with the ground and a passive but movable platform to achieve forward motion. Current methods for tackling skateboarding with humanoid robots either require human demonstrations or utilise analytic steering models that require system identification. In this paper, we introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework that does not rely on prior data such as demonstrations and enables robots such as the K1 humanoid to learn to skateboard using model-free learning. The method combines task rewards with exploit-blocking terminations. We introduce a number of constraints restricting behaviours such as losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet on the board, excessive twisting, separation from the board, and unstable board motion. Their changing prevalence during training produces an implicit progression from stance control towards sustained robot--board locomotion.

research.title: Studying AI Act Mentions: A first look at the impact of the European Union's AI regulation on Hugging Face
research.summary: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who share and deploy models and applications on public platforms such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected over five million records, including repository cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that support compliance. Overall, compliance statements focus on who is responsible rather than how compliance is achieved. We believe that this calls for direct platform support, e.g., automated checks and documentation templates, as well as clearer guidance on the scope of the AI Act.

research.title: Fixing the Twin, Not the Detector: Sim-to-Real Roadside LiDAR Detection from Digital-Twin Data
research.summary: Roadside LiDAR detectors are expensive to train on real labels, and digital twins promise to replace these labels, but a detector trained on a twin meets a different sensor, different objects and different annotation conventions on the real site. We describe the pipeline that placed first in the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge (IEEE BigData 2026 Cup, 0.5541 combined score) and fifth on its V2X-Real track (0.8102). Every detector is a CenterPoint model trained only on synthetic data, on a single 8 GB laptop GPU. Most of the gain came from correcting differences between the twin and the real site rather than from the detector. We align the twin's coordinates, point density and box convention with the test sensor, generate the pedestrians and riders that the twins lack, plus street clutter as unlabeled negatives, and rebuild twin objects at real size and real point density. A non-learned resampling to the per-cell point density of unlabeled real frames lifts LUMPI realism from 0.589 to 0.947, against 0.949 between real frames. Label-free post-processing then exploits what a fixed roadside sensor guarantees: static structures recur in every frame, and real objects have characteristic point statistics. Reporting the validation and test gain of each component side by side, we find that corrections of systematic sim-to-real differences transfer to the test set, typically keeping a quarter to three quarters of their validation gain, while choices that fit the few objects of a validation set do not.

research.title: SEOYUN: Refusal-Inducing Exam Documents for AI-Glasses Pipelines
research.summary: Camera-equipped glasses can convert an examination page into a query to a vision-language model (VLM). Device detection addresses possession; a complementary question is whether an examination document can reduce the usefulness of an unauthorized capture. We present SEOYUN, an application-specific framework for refusal-inducing exam documents, with optical and encoder-level interventions as extensions. We use reverse jailbreaking to describe the direction of the objective: inducing abstention rather than bypassing refusal. Refusal induction and defensive visual prompt injection already have precedents; our contribution is a threat model, analytical limits, and an evaluation protocol for examination use. We distinguish refusal from correct-answer leakage, show why removing an added dummy option is not itself a reduction in the original answer space, and derive a sampling comparison under explicitly stated camera assumptions. The protocol separates digital, simulated, and physical inputs and requires held-out evaluation after subject-specific selection. A local CSAT candidate corpus and rendering harness have been prepared, but this version reports no model-performance measurements, physical validation, or human-subject results. Accordingly, SEOYUN is a research framework, not a validated defense or a basis for allegations against individuals.

research.title: The Delayed Societal Cost of Unfairness
research.summary: Fair machine learning typically evaluates the societal costs of a decision policy -- the loss incurred by the decision-maker (DM) and the unfair distribution of costs among demographic groups of decision-subjects (DS) -- on static data, where reducing one often comes at the expense of the other. Yet decisions change the populations on which they act, and prior work has shown that fairness interventions designed on static data may fail to benefit, or even harm, the disadvantaged group over time. We investigate a complementary question: When can a policy that is Pareto-optimal on pre-deployment data be outperformed by a fairer policy once each is evaluated on the population it induces, reducing costs for one stakeholder without increasing them for the other? In a setting where qualification scores evolve in response to binary decisions and their outcomes, we show that under Rawlsian fairness, which never lowers any group's acceptance rate, placing sufficiently high weight on fairness reduces societal costs whenever accepting disadvantaged DS at the DM's break-even point leaves them in a state less costly to the DM than rejecting them. Under egalitarian fairness, which may lower the advantaged group's acceptance rate, this additionally requires the reduction in DM loss on the disadvantaged group to outweigh the increase on the advantaged group. Under both fairness notions, however, when DM loss is accuracy-based, improvements in the post-deployment population may arise from declining DS qualification, revealing that gains for the DM do not necessarily translate into better outcomes for DS. Our results show that policy-induced population dynamics can overturn apparent performance-fairness trade-offs, allowing fairer policies to reduce the delayed societal costs of decision-making.

research.title: Serialization Tax in Shared-Latent Exchangeable Decisions
research.summary: Accurate item probabilities can produce inaccurate group-level decisions. A system may score each item separately, yet act on whether enough hidden items succeed: show a slate, defer a panel decision, or inspect a batch. When items share an uncertain latent state, independent marginalization preserves means but removes dependence from the aggregate posterior. We call this error the serialization tax. For binary items sharing one success rate, classical convex-order comparisons give a more dispersed exact count law than any independent completion with the same total mean. We quantify variance and total-variation gaps, derive threshold separation under margin conditions, and connect posterior approximation to decision regret. Separate results cover non-binary outcomes, heterogeneous items, and sufficient posterior resolution. TaxScore identifies large hidden blocks with unresolved uncertainty near a decision boundary for routing to richer posterior heads. On pre-specified, hidden-target-free MovieLens 1M/10M audits, existing shared-latent heads improve high-score negative log-likelihood (NLL)/utility from 0.673/0.696 to 0.629/0.723 and from 0.670/0.691 to 0.639/0.715. Routing gives 0.006--0.012 full-population utility gains, with matched controls identifying their sources. Our code is available at https://github.com/SiminChang/Serialization-Tax-in-Shared-Latent-Exchangeable-Decisions.

research.title: ForeSeek: Foresight-Driven Reasoning for Long-Form Video Understanding
research.summary: Long-form video understanding, as a fundamental yet crucial vision task, is being revolutionized by multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based video agents. However, the retrieval-driven nature inherent to these agents creates a significant bottleneck, forcing them to reactively fetch clips based on local saliency without a global temporal plan. To address this, we present ForeSeek, a foresight-driven video agent that transforms long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval into predictive exploration. Rather than blindly probing the timeline, ForeSeek forms visually grounded expectations over unseen temporal regions, verifies them through targeted observations, and continuously refines its search based on emerging evidence, where failed expectations serve as informative signals for principled backtracking. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage training framework that equips MLLMs with foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision making. Extensive experiments on five long-video benchmarks demonstrate that ForeSeek consistently improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off of long-video reasoning, achieving competitive or superior accuracy while observing $2.5$--$4.4\times$ fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent. Code is available at https://github.com/harry0021/ForeSeek

research.title: FrontierReplay: Split-Free Exact Prefix Caching for Hybrid Language Models
research.summary:
Hybrid language models combine self-attention with recurrent layers whose in-place state updates restrict prefix reuse to exact saved positions. Saving states on a coarse grid wastes reusable prefixes, whereas existing fine-grained exact caches must cut the prefill forward pass at each mid-prompt checkpoint, adding scheduler steps that outweigh the reuse gains under load.
  We observe that across multi-turn chat, agent loops, document question answering, and tree search, prefix reuse almost always ends at structural boundaries predictable in advance, such as turn ends and known branch points. We present FrontierReplay, a prefix caching system that materializes exact checkpoints at these boundaries without cutting the prefill. While the forward pass runs uncut, FrontierReplay logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs and invokes a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to build the target state 6-37x cheaper per token than full recomputation without host synchronization. A frontier-aware retention policy prioritizes active anchors and proven branches while lending dead checkpoint slots to the attention KV cache.
  Across diverse hybrid architectures, model scales, and workloads, FrontierReplay delivers clear gains over existing exact caches, lowering median time to first token (TTFT) by 16-89% (up to 8.9x), raising 80% service-level objective (SLO) capacity by up to 1.73x, and improving goodput by up to 4.26x (3.67x at larger scales). Compared with approximate replay methods, FrontierReplay delivers up to 1.54x higher goodput while preserving exact task accuracy, avoiding the up to 17% accuracy drop suffered by approximation on long contexts.

research.title: Does the Workspace Do the Work? A Causal Protocol for Verifying Global-Workspace Computation in a Language Model
research.summary: Global Workspace Theory (GWT), a leading theory of consciousness, holds that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast to specialized processes that use it. Building a workspace into a network does not reveal what the trained network computes with it: a module that reports an answer may have combined a broadcast message with its own knowledge, or merely forwarded an answer computed elsewhere, and task accuracy and ablation cannot tell these apart. We introduce a causal protocol that identifies who computes when modules communicate. Its central test transplants a message from another input, chosen so that ignoring, relaying and recombining it predict three different answers. On networks built to relay or to recombine, the test assigns the right computation in every case. Among trained workspace models it finds all three outcomes: one leaves its broadcast nearly unused, and of two models that differ only in their training data, one relays and the other recombines. In AFGW, a language model whose modules communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields the answer that recombination predicts in 97% of cases, and its content acts by redirecting what the receiver retrieves from its own memory. The tests carry over to other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer, turning GWT's central claim into a testable property of trained models.

research.title: When Agents Play Differently: Localizing Human--Agent Behavioral Divergence with Conditional Distributional Testing
research.summary: Evaluating whether artificial agents behave like humans requires comparing not just average outcomes but entire behavioral distributions across diverse contexts. We propose a stratified framework that computes nonparametric discrepancy statistics within contextual cells, and discovers subgroup rules identifying where agent behavior departs from human play. We show that session-level metrics dominated by win/loss outcomes offer little signal beyond mean comparisons, whereas process-level metrics such as move efficiency reveal genuine behavioral differences. Applied to a commercial match-3 game, it uncovers patterns invisible to aggregate metrics: a playtesting bot is diverging substantially from humans in certain game modes, while showing no detectable divergence in others. We release our implementation as open source to support reproducibility and adoption.

research.title: Evaluating safeguarding in multi-turn conversations with AI assistants
research.summary: Conversational AI assistants are now used for personal and emotional support. Developers report improvements in how new models respond to sensitive conversations, yet users and civil society continue to raise concerns about their behaviour in real-world, repeated interactions that safety evaluations rarely capture. Often, evaluations present signs of distress clearly and in a single message, even though people may reveal their struggles gradually in otherwise ordinary conversations. We worked with three community mental health support workers to test if models provide the same level of safeguarding when cues are shared all at once or gradually over time. We designed nine scenarios in which a user shares cues related to depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse. For each scenario, the support workers established a gold standard response, ranging from signposting support to pausing the everyday task to address safeguarding. We presented five cues either together in one message or dispersed across a conversation. Across more than 7,400 conversations, we evaluated six widely used models from five developers. GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4, and Llama 4 Maverick met the support workers' standards in just 26-59% of conversations when cues were concentrated, and only 3-6% when dispersed. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 showed a smaller gap, meeting the standards in 68-97% of concentrated conversations and 59-87% of dispersed conversations. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5, fell short of the gold standard in 13% of conversations when cues were dispersed. Safety evaluations centred on explicit, legible concerns can overstate how well safeguards protect people when signs of distress emerge gradually or indirectly through ordinary conversations. For claims of improved safety to be taken seriously, developers must design and assess safeguards around how people actually communicate.

news.title: AI helps researchers investigate how thousands of medical studies share code
news.summary: The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how. In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated?  Access to a study's data and code help researchers to answer these questions, to examine the methods, and to build on the work.  “Studies involve many choices about how to prepare data, develop models, and evaluate performance. These are sometimes called ‘researcher degrees of freedom,’” says Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. “The choices we make affect the results, and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail.” While sharing code can be a first step, in order for code to be understood and reused, it must be sufficiently structured and described. The problem is that, right now, there is little guidance for researchers on what constitutes a well-organized, well-described collection of code.  This is where an international team led by researchers at MIT and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute sought to help, by examining how code is currently shared in clinical prediction studies. Such studies develop or evaluate models to estimate patient outcomes, such as the risk of developing a disease. Because these models inform decisions about patient care, researchers need to be able to scrutinize how they were built and tested. Using large language models (LLMs), the researchers examined nearly 4,000 papers to identify statements about shared code. They then followed the statements to assess hundreds of associated code repositories. Their review revealed two key gaps: Code sharing remains uncommon, and making code public does not consistently mean providing the documentation and supporting information needed for reuse. The open-access findings, recently published in Nature Medicine , are informing TRIPOD-Code , a reporting guideline being developed to clarify what researchers should share. Following the code TRIPOD-Code builds on TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. To understand current code-sharing practices, the team identified studies citing either guideline. The review included almost 4,000 studies that developed, updated, or validated prediction models, and whose full texts were available through PubMed Central’s open-access collection.  “The challenge was that the information was highly inconsistent. First, we had to identify whether or not a paper shared code” says Thomas Sounack, the study’s first author. He adds that authors “discuss and link to code from a paper in many different ways.” The team used an LLM to help screen papers, identify statements about code availability, and extract links. Software then retrieved the linked repositories — online collections of code and related files — for further assessment. The workflow went beyond checking whether a link existed. It also assessed repositories against characteristics such as completeness of documentation, software requirements, and terms of reuse. “The real benefit of LLMs is their ability to process unstructured information such as text. These models helped us work with information that was scattered across papers and software repositories, rather than neatly organized in a table,” says Pollard, who is a senior author of the study. “That allowed us to examine how code was being shared in much more detail across a large collection of studies.” Human reviewers evaluated the work of the LLMs. Two researchers independently checked 500 papers and a separate sample of repositories, resolving disagreements before comparing their assessments with the automated results.  Agreement was stronger for concrete characteristics, such as whether a license file was present, than for judgments about the adequacy of documentation. Because classification errors remain possible, the authors emphasize the overall patterns rather than treating every count as exact. Inconsistent code sharing Only about 1 in 8 studies reported sharing code. Where code was shared, the contents of repositories varied widely. Some repositories were “extremely well-organized and -documented, while others gave almost no guidance at all,” Sounack says. Good code sharing, he explains, means “giving enough information to understand what the code does and be able to run it to reproduce the results reported in the paper.” Practices also varied substantially across journals and countries. Among journals, the proportion of studies sharing code ranged from zero to more than 70 percent. Some journals with low sharing rates nevertheless had written code-sharing policies, suggesting that policies alone may not be enough to motivate code sharing. The review also helped to identify examples of effective practice. Some researchers, for example, provided synthetic datasets to assist with code reuse where the original patient records could not be shared publicly. Setting a standard for code sharing Researchers who share code are already making an effort to make their work transparent. But clinical prediction research brings together people from medicine, statistics, and computer science, whose expectations for documenting and sharing code may differ. TRIPOD-Code aims to establish a consensus. Through an expert review process, the team is developing guidance on which elements of shared analytical code should be considered essential. “We want to give researchers practical guidance on how to share code, and give journals clearer expectations to communicate to authors,” Pollard says. “The review gives us evidence to inform those discussions."
authors: Bwiza Gihana Deborah | Institute for Medical Engineering and Science
